items.text: The death of a tyrant is a fit occasion for public rejoicing.
items.evidence: The dragon devours Farquaad mid-speech ("I will have order! I will have perfection!"); Donkey quips "Celebrity marriages. They never last, do they?" and the town celebration follows.

items.text: Errors made in good faith deserve forgiveness rather than punishment.
items.evidence: "I'm sorry... Can you forgive me?" / "Hey, that's what friends are for, right?" and "that's what friends do! They forgive each other!"

items.text: Some beings are evil by their very constitution, rather than made so by circumstances that might be reasoned with or reformed.
items.evidence: Ogres are assumed constitutionally monstrous ("They'll make a suit from your freshly peeled skin"), but "there's a lot more to ogres than people think" / "ogres have layers."

items.text: Courage consists in the absence of fear.
items.evidence: Donkey: "there's nothing wrong with being afraid. Fear's a sensible response to an unfamiliar situation... it sure doesn't mean you're a coward if you're a little scared."

items.text: A person's moral character is legible in their outward appearance.
items.evidence: "They judge me before they even know me." / "Maybe you shouldn't judge people before you get to know them." / "Sometimes things are more than they appear." The monstrous-looking ogre is the hero; the handsome lord is the villain.

items.text: Physical beauty and vigour are outward signs of inner moral worth.
items.evidence: Farquaad: "beautiful, fair, flawless Fiona... the perfect bride for the perfect groom" — yet he is the tyrant; Fiona ends ogre-formed and Shrek says "But you are beautiful."

items.text: Being excluded on grounds of birth or race is a genuine injury rather than a slight imagined by the oversensitive.
items.evidence: Fairy tale creatures rounded up, bought and sold, sent to a "designated resettlement facility"; Shrek: "People take one look at me and go, Aah! Help! Run! A big, stupid, ugly ogre!"

items.text: Dignity and worth belong to the outcast and the diseased as fully as to anyone else.
items.evidence: The caged, sold "freaks" — talking donkey, gingerbread man, Pinocchio — are sympathetic; Donkey: "You don't know what it's like to be considered a freak... that's why we gotta stick together."

items.text: Someone born marked as different is thereby owed suspicion, and their exclusion is a natural consequence rather than an injustice.
items.evidence: Farquaad: "You and the rest of that fairy tale trash, poisoning my perfect world" is voiced by the villain; the film sides with the excluded.

items.text: Wealth and social standing confer a right to direct the lives of others.
items.evidence: Farquaad evicts the fairy tale creatures by decree and orders Fiona "locked back in that tower for the rest of your days"; he is devoured for it.

items.text: Marriage across differences of rank is a proper basis for a union.
items.evidence: "An ogre and a princess!" is Farquaad's derision; the film ends with their union celebrated.

items.text: Great authority, examined closely, is generally an apparatus of illusion rather than genuine power.
items.evidence: "Technically you're not a king"; the enormous castle prompts "Do you think maybe he's compensating for something?" — Farquaad's grandeur is shown as facade.

items.text: A person's moral character can be reliably inferred from their public reputation.
items.evidence: Ogres' reputation ("Grab your torch and pitchforks") is false to Shrek's character; Donkey: "Doesn't that bother you? Nope."

items.text: An orderly and decent community is preferable to one that is exciting and permissive.
items.evidence: DuLoc anthem: "Here we have some rules... Don't make waves, stay in line... DuLoc is a perfect place" — sung by animatronic puppets and played as sinister farce.

items.text: Becoming a better person requires smoothing away one's rough edges and becoming uniformly agreeable.
items.evidence: Shrek remains crude to the end ("Better out than in, I always say"), and Fiona ends as an ogre rather than being smoothed into the princess ideal.

items.text: A person should present to the world the self that others require of them, whatever the inward cost.
items.evidence: Fiona hides her night form to be "the perfect bride"; the happy ending comes only when she is seen as she is.

items.text: A person's first duty is to discover and express what is genuinely inside them, rather than to fulfil the role assigned by family and institution.
items.evidence: Fiona: "I'm a princess, and this is not how a princess is meant to look" — the assigned script is abandoned for her true form, "But you are beautiful."

items.text: Romantic love arising suddenly between strangers is a sufficient foundation for the deepest of bonds.
items.evidence: The rescue-and-instant-kiss script ("You were meant to charge in, sword drawn, banner flying") is mocked; love grows over the journey instead.

items.text: True love is recognized immediately and requires no knowledge of the other's name or origin.
items.evidence: Fiona insists "it's destiny... they share true love's first kiss" with a rescuer she has never met; the film corrects her — the true love is the ogre she came to know.

items.text: Solitude and emotional guardedness are a diminishment to be moved past, not a stable way of living.
items.evidence: Shrek: "That's why I'm better off alone" and "build a ten-foot wall around my land"; Donkey names it as hiding, and Shrek finally abandons the wall for love and friendship.

items.text: Friendship freely given to strangers, without prior obligation, is among the highest goods.
items.evidence: Donkey attaches himself to a stranger with no obligation: "I'll stick with you"; "Because that's what friends do! They forgive each other!" and the film's resolution depends on that friendship.

items.text: Refusing help and relying wholly on oneself is a strength.
items.evidence: "I live alone! My swamp! Me! Nobody else!" is presented as Shrek's wound, not his strength; he reverses it.

items.text: Those in command may legitimately spend the lives of the people under them as a calculated price for information or advantage.
items.evidence: Farquaad to the knights: "Some of you may die, but it's a sacrifice I am willing to make" — delivered as the villain's self-serving absurdity.

items.text: Reaching out to another in trust carries real risk, and the risk is worth taking.
items.evidence: Shrek risks exposure — "I object!" and "I love you" — after being afraid of being seen; the risk is rewarded.

items.text: Cynicism about human motives is a truer view of the world than sentimentality.
items.evidence: Shrek's cynicism ("Like that's ever gonna happen. What a load of...") is the position the film dismantles, ending on "Now I'm a believer."

items.text: Courage is not the absence of fear but acting while afraid for the sake of another.
items.evidence: Donkey crosses the lava bridge terrified ("I'm gonna die") and later confronts the guards: "I'm a donkey on the edge!" for Shrek's sake.

items.text: Telling the truth restores what deception has damaged.
items.evidence: Fiona's concealment ("Promise you won't tell") produces the rupture; Donkey — "What's the point of being able to talk if you gotta keep secrets?" — and the revealed truth restores things.

layers.label: Plot summary
layers.content:
## Plot
Shrek is an asocial ogre who loves the solitude of his swamp and enjoys fending off mobs and intruders. One day, his life is interrupted after he inadvertently saves a talkative Donkey from some soldiers, prompting Donkey to forcibly stay with him. Donkey is one of many fairy tale creatures that are being exiled by the dwarfish Lord Farquaad of Duloc to beautify his land. However, the creatures inadvertently end up in the swamp. Angered by the intrusion, Shrek resolves to visit Farquaad and demand that he move the creatures elsewhere, reluctantly allowing Donkey to accompany him as he is the only one who knows where Duloc is.
Meanwhile, Farquaad asks a magic mirror if he has the most perfect kingdom; the mirror tells him he is not a king and would need to marry a princess in order to become one. Presented with three options, Farquaad chooses Princess Fiona, who is imprisoned in a castle guarded by a Dragon. Unwilling to rescue Fiona himself, he organizes a tournament, the winner receiving the "privilege" of rescuing her on his behalf. When Farquaad sees Shrek and Donkey in his castle, he announces that whoever kills Shrek will win the tournament; however, Shrek and Donkey defeat Farquaad's knights with relative ease. Amused, Farquaad proclaims Shrek his champion, and agrees to relocate the fairy tale creatures in exchange for Shrek rescuing Fiona.
Shrek and Donkey travel to the castle and Dragon attacks them. Shrek locates Fiona, who is bewildered by his lack of romanticism; they flee the castle after rescuing Donkey from Dragon, who is revealed to be female and has fallen in love with him. When Shrek removes his helmet and reveals he is an ogre, Fiona stubbornly refuses to go to Duloc, demanding Farquaad arrive in person to save her, but Shrek carries Fiona against her will. That night, after setting up camp, and with Fiona alone in a cave, Shrek admits to Donkey that he is asocial because he grew frustrated over being constantly judged for his appearance. Fiona overhears this and becomes kinder to Shrek. The next day, Robin Hood and his band of Merry Men harass the three, but Fiona easily defeats them in physical combat. Shrek becomes impressed with Fiona, and they begin to fall in love.
When the trio nears Duloc, Fiona takes shelter in a windmill for the evening. Donkey enters alone and discovers that Fiona has transformed into an ogress. She explains that during her childhood, she was cursed to transform into an ogress at night but retain her human form during the day. She tells Donkey that only "true love's first kiss" will break the spell and allow her to "take love's true form". Meanwhile, Shrek is about to confess his feelings to Fiona, when he overhears Fiona referring to herself as an "ugly beast". Thinking that she is talking about him, Shrek angrily leaves and returns the next morning with Farquaad. Confused and hurt by Shrek's abrupt hostility, Fiona reluctantly accepts Farquaad's marriage proposal and requests that they be married that day before sunset. Shrek dismisses Donkey and returns to his now vacated swamp, but quickly realizes that he feels miserable without Fiona. Donkey returns and lectures Shrek for jumping to conclusions and reveals that Fiona was not referring to him as an "ugly beast", although Donkey does not reveal Fiona's secret to Shrek. The two reconcile, and Donkey summons Dragon, whom he had reunited with earlier in the day. Shrek and Donkey ride Dragon to Duloc so they can stop the wedding.
Shrek interrupts the ceremony just before it ends and expresses his feelings for Fiona. The sun sets, and Fiona transforms into an ogress in front of everyone. Disgusted and enraged, Farquaad orders Shrek to be executed and Fiona re-imprisoned, while he declares himself king. The two are saved when Dragon, ridden by Donkey, breaks in and devours Farquaad. Shrek and Fiona kiss, and Fiona's curse is broken; though she remains an ogress, Shrek reassures her that he still finds her beautiful. They marry in the swamp with the fairy tale creatures in attendance, then leave for their honeymoon.

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Response
In addition to being an instant box office success, Shrek received wide critical acclaim. 88% of 212 professional reviews of the film on the review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes are positive, with an average rating of 7.8/10. The website's critical consensus reads, "While simultaneously embracing and subverting fairy tales, the irreverent Shrek also manages to tweak Disney's nose, provide a moral message to children, and offer viewers a funny, fast-paced ride." Metacritic assigned Shrek a weighted average score of 84 out of 100 based on 34 critics, indicating "universal acclaim". Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an average grade of "A" on an A+ to F scale.

Roger Ebert praised the film, giving it four stars out of a possible four and describing it as "jolly and wicked, filled with sly in-jokes and yet somehow possessing a heart". USA Today's Susan Wloszczyna praised Eddie Murphy's performance, stating it "gives the comic performance of his career, aided by sensational digital artistry, as he brays for the slightly neurotic motormouth". Richard Schickel of Time also enjoyed Murphy's role, stating "No one has ever made a funnier jackass of himself than Murphy." Peter Rainer of New York magazine liked the script, also stating "The animation, directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, is often on the same wriggly, giggly level as the script, although the more "human" characters, such as Princess Fiona and Lord Farquaad, are less interesting than the animals and creatures—a common pitfall in animated films of all types." Peter Travers of Rolling Stone wrote "Shrek is a world-class charmer that could even seduce the academy when it hands out the first official animation Oscar next year." James Berardinelli of ReelViews gave the film three and a half stars out of four, saying "Shrek is not a guilty pleasure for sophisticated movie-goers; it is, purely and simply, a pleasure." Kenneth Turan of the Los Angeles Times wrote "The witty, fractured fairy tale Shrek has a solid base of clever writing." Lisa Schwarzbaum of Entertainment Weekly gave the film an A−, saying "A kind of palace coup, a shout of defiance, and a coming of age for DreamWorks." Jay Boyar of the Orlando Sentinel wrote "It's a pleasure to be able to report that the movie both captures and expands upon the book's playful spirit of deconstruction."
Steven Rosen of The Denver Post wrote "DreamWorks Pictures again proves a name to trust for imaginative, funny animated movies that delight kids and adults equally." Susan Stark of The Detroit News gave the film four out of four stars, saying "Swift, sweet, irreverent, rangy and as spirited in the writing and voice work as it is splendid in design." Jami Bernard of the New York Daily News gave the film four out of four stars, saying "The brilliance of the voice work, script, direction and animation all serve to make Shrek an adorable, infectious work of true sophistication." Rene Rodriguez gave the film three out of four stars, calling it "a gleefully fractured fairy tale that never becomes cynical or crass". Elvis Mitchell of The New York Times gave the film four out of five stars, saying "Beating up on the irritatingly dainty Disney trademarks is nothing new; it's just that it has rarely been done with the demolition-derby zest of Shrek." William Steig, the author of the original book, and his wife Jeanne Steig also enjoyed the film, stating "We all went sort of expecting to hate it, thinking, 'What has Hollywood done to it?' But we loved it. We were afraid it would be too sickeningly cute and, instead, Bill just thought they did a wonderful, witty job of it."
John Anderson of Newsday wrote "The kind of movie that will entertain everyone of every age and probably for ages to come." Jay Carr of The Boston Globe wrote "In an era when much on film seems old, Shrek seems new and fresh and clever." Stephen Hunter of The Washington Post gave the film five out of five stars, saying "Despite all its high-tech weirdness, it is really that most perdurable of human constructions, a tale told well and true." Joe Baltake of The Sacramento Bee wrote that it "isn't so much a fractured spoof of everything Disney, but actually a Monty Python flick for kids – kids of all ages". Andrew Sarris of The New York Observer wrote "What gives Shrek its special artistic distinction is its witty and knowingly sassy dialogue, delivered by vocally charismatic performers whose voices remind us of their stellar screen personae in live-action movies." Lisa Alspector of the Chicago Reader wrote "This romantic fantasy complicates the roles of beauty and beast, making it hard to guess what form a sensitive resolution will take." Joe Morgenstern of The Wall Street Journal wrote "The charms of Shrek, which is based on the children's book by William Steig, go far beyond in-jokes for adults." John Zebrowski of The Seattle Times gave the film three out of four stars, saying "The movie is helped immensely by its cast, who carry it through some of the early, sluggish scenes. But this is Murphy's movie. Donkey gets most of the good lines, and Murphy hits every one."
A mixed review came from Mark Caro of the Chicago Tribune, who gave the film two and a half stars out of four and compared it to Toy Story 2, which he said "had a higher in-jokes/laughs ratio without straining to demonstrate its hipness or to evoke heartfelt emotions". On the more negative side, Michael Atkinson of The Village Voice said he was "desperately avoiding the risk of even a half-second of boredom", and said "the movie is wall-to-window-to-door noise, babbling, and jokes (the first minute sees the first fart gag), and demographically it's a hard-sell shotgun spray." Christy Lemire of the Associated Press described Shrek as a "90-minute onslaught of in-jokes", and said while it "strives to have a heart" with "a message about beauty coming from within", "somehow [the message] rings hollow". Anthony Lane of The New Yorker said, despite the film "cunning the rendering of surfaces, there's still something flat and charmless in the digital look, and most of the pleasure rises not from the main romance but from the quick, incidental gags."

## Legacy > Rank
Entertainment Weekly put Shrek on its end-of-the-decade "best-of" list for the 2000s, saying, "Prince Charming? So last millennium. This decade, fairy-tale fans – and Princess Fiona – fell for a fat and flatulent Ogre. Now, that's progress."  In June 2008, the American Film Institute revealed its "Ten top Ten"; the best ten films in ten "classic" American film genres—after polling over 1,500 people from the creative community Shrek was acknowledged as the eighth best film in the animated genre, and the only non-Disney·Pixar film in the Top 10. Shrek was also ranked second in a Channel 4 poll of the "100 Greatest Family Films", losing out on the top spot to E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial. In 2005, Shrek came sixth in Channel 4's 100 Greatest Cartoons poll behind The Simpsons, Tom and Jerry, South Park, Toy Story and Family Guy. In November 2009, the character, Lord Farquaad, was listed No. 14 in IGN UK's "Top 15 Fantasy Villains". In 2006, it was ranked third on Bravo's 100 funniest films list. The film's title character was awarded his own star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in May 2010.

AFI's 100 Years...100 Heroes & Villains:
Shrek – Nominated Hero
AFI's 100 Years...100 Songs:
"I'm a Believer" – Nominated
AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition) – Nominated
AFI's 10 Top 10 – No. 8 Animated film

## Legacy > Cultural Impact
The New York Times retrospectively described the film as "a beloved, offbeat fairy tale whose characters and jokes continue to permeate pop culture, reaching another generation of fans." Previous films and television shows, such as Fractured Fairy Tales and The Princess Bride, had parodied the traditional fairy tale. Shrek had a significant impact that influenced a later generation of mainstream animated films, receiving recognition for being one of the most influential from the 2000s. Animated films such as Ice Age and Despicable Me began to incorporate more pop culture references. It also inspired a number of computer animated films which also spoofed fairy tales, or other related story genres, often including adult-oriented humor, such as Happily N'Ever After, Hoodwinked!, and Enchanted. In 2020, the United States Library of Congress selected Shrek to be preserved in the National Film Registry for being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".
